## Abstract

This session examines **trade**: the classical case for free trade, from Smith and Ricardo,
and the challenges to it — unequal terms of trade, technological lock-in, and the
**externalization** of ecological costs across countries. The second part of the session
turns to the **environmental conflicts** this produces on the ground (see
[Environmental conflicts](s_05b_Conflicts.html)).

## The computations behind the trade examples (slides 8–12)

### 1. Adam Smith: absolute advantage (slides 8–9)

**The setup.** Germany 🇩🇪 and Japan 🇯🇵 each have **100 units of labour (L)**. If a
country uses *all* of its labour on one good, it can produce:

|    | L   | 🥨 (all labour) | 🍱 (all labour) |
|----|-----|-----------------|-----------------|
| 🇩🇪 | 100 | 20              | 10              |
| 🇯🇵 | 100 | 16              | 12              |

From this follows how much labour one unit of each good costs:

- 🇩🇪: one 🥨 costs $100/20 = 5$ L, one 🍱 costs $100/10 = 10$ L.
- 🇯🇵: one 🥨 costs $100/16 = 6.25$ L, one 🍱 costs $100/12 \approx 8.33$ L.

So 🇩🇪 is absolutely better at pretzels (5 L < 6.25 L) and 🇯🇵 is absolutely better
at bento (8.33 L < 10 L). Each country has an **absolute advantage** in one good.

**Relative value.** The last column of the slide's left table shows what one pretzel is
worth *within* each country, measured in bento. In 🇩🇪, the labour for one 🥨 (5 L)
could instead produce half a 🍱 ($5/10 = 0.5$). In 🇯🇵, the labour for one 🥨 (6.25 L)
could produce $6.25/8.33 = 0.75$ 🍱. Equivalently, divide the two production
possibilities: $10/20 = 0.5$ and $12/16 = 0.75$.

**No trade.** Without trade, each country must produce both goods itself. The slide
assumes that each country splits its labour evenly, 50 L per good:

- 🇩🇪: $50/5 = 10$ 🥨 and $50/10 = 5$ 🍱
- 🇯🇵: $50/6.25 = 8$ 🥨 and $50/8.33 = 6$ 🍱
- World (🇺🇳): $10 + 8 = 18$ 🥨 and $5 + 6 = 11$ 🍱

**Trade.** Now each country puts all its labour into the good in which it has the
absolute advantage: 🇩🇪 makes 20 🥨 and no 🍱; 🇯🇵 makes 12 🍱 and no 🥨. World output
rises to 20 🥨 and 12 🍱, which is **2 🥨 and 1 🍱 more** than before. Not a single
extra hour was worked: the gain comes entirely from the division of labour.

|    | No trade 🥨 | No trade 🍱 | Trade 🥨 | Trade 🍱 | Change 🥨 | Change 🍱 |
|----|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|
| 🇩🇪 | 10  | 5   | 20  | 0   | +10 | −5  |
| 🇯🇵 | 8   | 6   | 0   | 12  | −8  | +6  |
| 🇺🇳 | 18  | 11  | 20  | 12  | +2  | +1  |

**The corridor in which both win (slide 9).** Specialisation alone leaves 🇩🇪 without
bento and 🇯🇵 without pretzels, so the two have to exchange. Suppose 🇩🇪 sends $x$ 🥨 to
🇯🇵 and receives $y$ 🍱 in return. Each country should end up with more of both goods
than it had without trade:

- 🇩🇪 keeps $20 - x$ 🥨, which must exceed 10, so $x < 10$; and it receives $y$ 🍱, which
  must exceed 5, so $y > 5$.
- 🇯🇵 receives $x$ 🥨, which must exceed 8, so $x > 8$; and it keeps $12 - y$ 🍱, which
  must exceed 6, so $y < 6$.

Hence $8 < x < 10$ and $5 < y < 6$. This is the slide's corridor: 🇩🇪 trades roughly
8.1–9.9 🥨 for 5.1–5.9 🍱. Within it, the $+2$ 🥨 and $+1$ 🍱 of extra world output are
shared between the two countries, and *how* they are shared depends on where in the
corridor the exchange lands.

Note how the corridor lines up with the relative values: the implied exchange rate $y/x$
lies between $5/10 = 0.5$ and $6/8 = 0.75$ bento per pretzel. That is, the price at which
the two countries trade must lie between their two domestic relative values. Below 0.5,
🇩🇪 would be better off making bento itself; above 0.75, the same holds for 🇯🇵 and
pretzels.

### 2. David Ricardo: comparative advantage (slides 10–12)

**The setup.** This is Ricardo's original example. The table now shows **labour
requirements**, i.e. how many hours it takes to produce *one* unit:

|        | 🍷 (wine) | 🧥 (cloth) |
|--------|-----------|------------|
| 🇵🇹     | 80        | 90         |
| 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿     | 120       | 100        |

Portugal needs fewer hours for *both* goods, so it has an absolute advantage in both.
On Smith's logic there would be no reason to trade. Ricardo shows that there is one
anyway.

**Who is *relatively* better at what (slide 11).** Compare Portugal's labour
requirements with England's, good by good:

- 🍷: $80/120 \approx 0.67$, so Portugal needs only 67% of England's labour.
- 🧥: $90/100 = 0.9$, so Portugal needs 90% of England's labour.

Portugal's lead is much larger in wine, so its comparative advantage lies in 🍷, and
England's (its *smallest disadvantage*) in 🧥.

**Opportunity costs.** The same result follows from asking what each country gives up.
The 90 hours Portugal spends on one 🧥 could instead produce $90/80 = 1.125$ 🍷. In
England, the 100 hours for one 🧥 could instead produce $100/120 \approx 0.833$ 🍷. So
cloth is relatively cheaper in England (it costs 0.833 🍷 there versus 1.125 🍷 in
Portugal), and by the same token wine is relatively cheaper in Portugal (it costs
$80/90 \approx 0.89$ 🧥 there versus $120/100 = 1.2$ 🧥 in England). Note that what
matters is *not* how many hours a good takes in absolute terms, but how much of the
other good one must forgo to produce it.

**No trade (slide 12).** Suppose each country produces one unit of each good:

- 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿: $120 + 100 = 220$ hours for 1 🍷 and 1 🧥
- 🇵🇹: $80 + 90 = 170$ hours for 1 🍷 and 1 🧥
- World: 2 🍷 and 2 🧥

**Specialisation.** Now each country uses the same hours only for the good in which it
has the comparative advantage:

- 🇵🇹: $170/80 = 2.125$ 🍷 and no 🧥
- 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿: $220/100 = 2.2$ 🧥 and no 🍷
- World: 2.125 🍷 and 2.2 🧥, which is **0.125 🍷 and 0.2 🧥 more** with the same total
  labour of 390 hours.

**The terms of trade.** As in Smith's case, the two countries must exchange. Suppose
England sends 1 🧥 to Portugal and receives $w$ 🍷 in return:

- 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 ends up with $2.2 - 1 = 1.2$ 🧥 and $w$ 🍷. It is better off than before if
  $w \geq 1$.
- 🇵🇹 ends up with 1 🧥 and $2.125 - w$ 🍷. It is better off than before if
  $2.125 - w > 1$, so $w < 1.125$.

Any exchange of 1 🧥 for between 1 and 1.125 🍷 thus leaves both countries with more
than they had without trade. More generally, the price of cloth must lie between the two
opportunity costs from above: above England's 0.833 🍷 (otherwise England would rather
make its own wine) and below Portugal's 1.125 🍷 (otherwise Portugal would rather make
its own cloth).

**The take-away.** Trade can be mutually beneficial even when one country is more
productive in everything. What drives the gains are differences in *opportunity costs*,
not in absolute productivity. This simple narrative remains at the core of many trade
debates and analyses, which is why it is worth looking closely at the assumptions built
into it: full employment, labour as the only input, no transport costs, and no
ecological costs of production or shipping.
